proof_skeleton_nl: Fix a prime p > 3 and define the inverse permutation I. Replace each index k by the pair (a,b) = (I(k)+1, I(k+1)-1). A direct modular calculation shows that this gives a bijection between k in {1,...,p-2} and the points (a,b) with 2 <= a <= p-1, 1 <= b <= p-2, and a*b ≡ -1 mod p. Under this bijection, the descent condition I(k+1) < I(k) becomes exactly the linear inequality b <= a-3. Hence the descent number D(p)=|S| is the number of points of the modular hyperbola ab ≡ -1 mod p lying in the convex triangular region R_p = {(a,b): 2 <= a <= p-1, 1 <= b <= a-3}. The area of R_p is ((p-4)^2)/2, so the expected main term for the hyperbola-point count is area(R_p)/p = p/2 - 4 + 8/p. A standard modular-hyperbola discrepancy estimate for convex regions implies that the actual count differs from this main term by at most C sqrt(p) log p for an absolute constant C. Since p/2 - 4 + 8/p dominates p/4 - 1 by a linear margin, the error term is negligible for all sufficiently large primes; therefore there exists P0 such that for every prime p >= P0 one has D(p) > p/4 - 1. The finitely many primes 5 <= p < P0 are then checked directly, yielding the stronger inequality D(p) >= floor(p/4). Combining the two ranges proves the theorem for every prime p > 3.

steps.derives: For the fixed prime p > 3 in the root theorem, the inverse map I : {1,...,p-1} -> {1,...,p-1} is well-defined by k * I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p).
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the existence-and-uniqueness statement of L1 specialized to the chosen prime p.

steps.derives: The map k ↦ (I(k)+1, I(k+1)-1) is a bijection from {1,...,p-2} onto the set T_p = { (a,b) : 2 <= a <= p-1, 1 <= b <= p-2, a*b ≡ -1 (mod p) }.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L2 with the already-defined inverse map I. This rewrites the consecutive-inverse data as points on the modular hyperbola ab ≡ -1 mod p with the correct endpoint ranges.

steps.derives: If R_p = { (a,b) in R^2 : 2 <= a <= p-1 and 1 <= b <= a-3 }, then D(p) = |S| = |T_p ∩ R_p|. Equivalently, |S| = |H_p ∩ R_p| because T_p is exactly H_p restricted to the same coordinate ranges and those ranges are already built into R_p.
steps.trivial_justification: L3 says that for each k, the descent condition I(k+1) < I(k) is equivalent to the inequality b <= a-3 for the associated pair (a,b). Combining this equivalence with the bijection from A2 identifies the descent count with the number of relevant hyperbola points inside R_p.

steps.derives: The region R_p is convex and area(R_p)/p = p/2 - 4 + 8/p.
There exists an absolute constant C > 0 such that for every prime p, ||H_p ∩ R_p| - (p/2 - 4 + 8/p)| <= C * sqrt(p) * log p.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L5 to the specific convex polygon R_p from A4 and substitute the explicit area formula from A4.

steps.derives: There exists an integer P0 >= 5 such that for every prime p >= P0, one has |H_p ∩ R_p| > p/4 - 1.
steps.trivial_justification: L6 is exactly the large-prime consequence of the discrepancy estimate established in A5.

steps.derives: For the same threshold P0, every prime p with 5 <= p < P0 satisfies |S| >= floor(p/4), hence |S| > p/4 - 1.
steps.trivial_justification: L7 handles the finite set of small primes. Since floor(p/4) is an integer strictly greater than p/4 - 1, the desired strict inequality follows immediately from |S| >= floor(p/4).

steps.derives: For every prime p >= P0, one has |S| > p/4 - 1.
steps.trivial_justification: From A3 we have |S| = |H_p ∩ R_p|. Substitute this identity into the large-prime bound from A6.

steps.derives: For every prime p > 3, if S = { k in {1,...,p-2} : I(k+1) < I(k) }, then |S| > p/4 - 1.
steps.trivial_justification: Every prime p > 3 satisfies p >= 5, so either p < P0 or p >= P0. Use A7 in the first case and A8 in the second case. This yields the root theorem exactly.
